question: What is an algorithm?
correct: A finite, step-by-step procedure for solving a problem
incorrect: A physical machine that runs computer programs for you
A programming language used to write modern software
A diagram showing how a computer's parts are wired up
feedback: An algorithm is a finite sequence of clear steps that solves a problem. It is the idea, independent of any machine or language that carries it out.

question: An {{1}} is the idea itself — a finite sequence of unambiguous steps that solves a problem — while a {{2}} is that same idea written down in a language some particular machine can actually run.
feedback: This is the distinction the whole chapter turns on. The algorithm outlives any machine or language: the same sorting algorithm can be written as a Python program, a Java program, or followed by hand with a deck of cards.

question: Computer scientists often say the central idea of the field is the algorithm, not the computer. Why?
correct: An algorithm is the idea; a computer is one machine that runs it
incorrect: A computer can carry out a procedure without any algorithm
An algorithm is written for one particular model of computer
Every algorithm has to be expressed in a programming language
feedback: Algorithms existed long before electronic computers. The same algorithm can be performed by a person, a gear-driven machine, or a modern CPU, which is why the idea, not the device, is central.

question: A part of an algorithm that repeats the same steps over and over is called a ___.
correct: loop
repetition
feedback: Repetition is what lets a short algorithm handle a long list: without it you would need one written step for every single item.

question: Which of the following are properties that every algorithm should have? (Select all that apply)
correct: It finishes after a finite number of steps
Each step is clearly and unambiguously defined
It produces a result for valid inputs
incorrect: It must be written in the Python language
It always runs in the same amount of time no matter the input
feedback: Algorithms must be finite, unambiguous, and produce output. They are language-independent, and their running time can grow with input size.

question: A student writes this step in a recipe algorithm: "Add some salt, then cook until it looks about right." Which requirement of a good algorithm does this step break?
correct: Every step must be unambiguous, with only one possible meaning
incorrect: Every step must finish after a limited number of repetitions
Every algorithm must take at least one input before it starts
Every algorithm must be written down before it can be tested
feedback: Two people following this step would do different things and get different results, which is exactly what an algorithm has to rule out. The step does end, so finiteness is not the problem, and plenty of useful algorithms take no input at all.

question: This loop multiplies as it counts down. What does it print?
code:
count = 5
result = 1
while count > 1:
    result = result * count
    count = count - 1
print(result)
feedback: Track both variables on each pass: result runs 1, 5, 20, 60, 120 while count runs 5, 4, 3, 2, 1, and the loop stops the moment count is no longer greater than 1. Starting result at 0 instead of 1 would have made every product 0.

question: Which of these everyday things are best described as algorithms? (Select all that apply)
correct: A recipe with ordered cooking steps
Turn-by-turn directions to a destination
incorrect: A grocery list with no instructions
A photo of a finished cake
A pile of unsorted ingredients
feedback: An algorithm is a sequence of steps. A recipe and directions give ordered steps; a list, a photo, or a pile gives no procedure to follow.

question: Arrange the steps into a correct algorithm for finding the largest number in a list.
items: Take the first number as the current largest
Compare the next number to the current largest
If the new number is bigger, make it the current largest
Repeat the comparison until no numbers remain
Report the current largest as the answer
feedback: An algorithm is a finite sequence of precise steps: start with a candidate, compare against every remaining item, update when you find something bigger, and report the result at the end.

question: In computer science, what does abstraction mean?
correct: Hiding unnecessary detail so you can focus on the important ideas
incorrect: Removing the comments from a program so that it will run faster
Translating an algorithm written in English directly into binary code
Drawing a flowchart of an algorithm instead of writing its pseudocode
feedback: Abstraction means ignoring irrelevant detail to manage complexity, like using a car's steering wheel without knowing how the engine works.

question: Calling print() without knowing how the screen lights individual pixels is an example of ___.
correct: abstraction
feedback: Abstraction lets you drive a car without thinking about the engine — and call print() without thinking about pixels.

question: A brute-force search solves a problem by:
correct: Systematically trying every possibility until the answer is found
incorrect: Trying random possibilities until time runs out, then reporting the best
Narrowing the search with a rule of thumb that skips unlikely options
Repeatedly halving the search range the way binary search does
feedback: Brute force checks every possible candidate. It is simple and guaranteed to find an answer if one exists, but it can be slow when there are many possibilities.

question: The 1880 US census took eight years to count by hand. What did Herman Hollerith's 1890 tabulating machines do differently?
correct: Each person became a punch card the machines counted electrically
incorrect: They asked their census questions of each household by telephone
They estimated the population from a small sample of households
They stored the whole census in memory and sorted it by program
feedback: Each person became one punch card. Metal pins passed through the holes to close an electrical circuit, advancing a counter. The 1890 count finished in a single year, and Hollerith's company later became IBM.

question: The punched-card counting machine Herman Hollerith built for the 1890 US census is called a ___ machine.
correct: tabulating
tabulator
tabulation
feedback: To tabulate is to count and group into a table, which is exactly what the machine did electrically with millions of cards, cutting a job measured in years down to a fraction of the time. Hollerith's company later became part of IBM.

question: Hollerith's machines grouped records by a category and counted each group. A Python dictionary stores values under named keys. Which use of one does the same job?
correct: A dictionary, mapping each category to its running count
incorrect: A single integer variable that stores the grand total
A string holding every category name joined together
A flowchart showing which category comes first
feedback: A dictionary stores values by key, so each category name maps to how many records had it. That is exactly what the tabulator's mechanical counters did, one counter per category.

question: You have written pseudocode for a task. What still has to happen before a computer can carry it out?
correct: It has to be translated into a real programming language
incorrect: It has to be redrawn as a flowchart before it will run
It has to be checked for spelling by a pseudocode checker
Nothing further, because a computer can run pseudocode directly
feedback: Pseudocode is written for humans, so no machine runs it. It is a plan you then translate — which is why the same pseudocode can become a Python program or a Java one.

question: What is the main purpose of a flowchart?
correct: To show an algorithm's steps and decisions visually with shapes and arrows
incorrect: To list an algorithm's steps in plain sentences without a diagram
To record the value each variable holds while the program runs
To rank an algorithm's steps by how much time each one takes
feedback: A flowchart represents an algorithm graphically: arrows show the order of steps, and shapes mark actions and decisions.

question: In a standard flowchart, which shape represents a decision (a yes/no question)?
correct: A diamond
incorrect: A rectangle
An oval
A parallelogram
feedback: A diamond marks a decision point with branching paths. Rectangles are processes, ovals are start/end, and parallelograms are input/output.

question: An informal, human-readable description of an algorithm's steps, not run by a computer, is called ___.
correct: pseudocode
pseudo-code
feedback: Pseudocode bridges plain language and real code, letting you plan logic before writing a program.

question: Match each line of pseudocode to the kind of action it describes.

pairs.definition: Stores a starting value in a variable
Chooses what happens next based on a condition
Repeats steps as long as something stays true
Reads a value supplied by the person running it
Displays a value to the person running it

feedback: Pseudocode has no official grammar, but these five actions — assignment, decision, repetition, input, and output — are enough to describe almost any algorithm before you commit to a real language.

question: Match each flowchart shape to what it represents.

pairs.definition: Marks the start or end of the process
Represents a single action or processing step
Poses a question that branches the path
Shows input being read or output being shown

feedback: Each flowchart shape has a fixed meaning, which is what lets people read one another's diagrams.

question: NPC: Tracing pseudocode, one line at a time
intro: A workshop door creaks open. A tinkerer looks up from a bench covered in gears and chalk. “New apprentice? Good. Before you fight anything, watch how I read a program the way the machine does — one line at a time.”

steps.say:
Here's a scrap of pseudocode:
SET count TO 10
ADD 5 TO count
SUBTRACT 2 FROM count
PRINT count
Don't guess the answer — trace it. Start at the top: SET count TO 10. I write count = 10 in the margin.

beats.code:
SET count TO 10
ADD 5 TO count
SUBTRACT 2 FROM count
PRINT count

beats.say: Don't guess the answer — trace it. Start at the top: SET count TO 10. I write count = 10 in the margin.

steps.say: Next line: ADD 5 TO count. The old value was 10, so the margin now says count = 15.

check.prompt: Next line: SUBTRACT 2 FROM count. What does the margin say now?
check.why: 15 minus 2 is 13. The margin always holds the latest value, not the history.

steps.say: Last line: PRINT count. Whatever the margin holds is what appears: 13. That's tracing — no guessing, just bookkeeping. Every variable is a box, and you track what's in the box.

outro: “Your turn. The monster ahead carries a scrap of pseudocode just like mine. Keep a margin.”

question: Pseudocode says: SET total TO 0; ADD 5 TO total; ADD 3 TO total; PRINT total. What is printed?
feedback: total starts at 0, becomes 5 after the first addition, then 8 after the second, so 8 is printed.

question: Read this pseudocode: SET x TO {{a}}; MULTIPLY x BY 2; SUBTRACT {{b}} FROM x; PRINT x. What number is printed?
feedback_template: Follow the lines in order, keeping track of x: it starts at {{a}}, doubles, and then loses {{b}}, leaving {{expected}}. Order matters — subtracting first would give a different answer.

question: What does this program output?
feedback: x holds 4 and y holds 10, so x + y is 14. The + operator adds the two numbers.

question: This loop keeps a running total. What does it output?
code:
total = 0
for n in [2, 4, 6]:
    total = total + n
print(total)
feedback: The loop adds 2, then 4, then 6 into total, which acts as an accumulator. 2 + 4 + 6 = 12.

question: What does this remainder calculation output?
feedback: The modulo operator % gives the remainder of division. 17 divided by 5 is 3 with a remainder of 2.

question: In a program, a variable that builds up a running total across a loop is commonly called a(n):
correct: Accumulator
incorrect: Loop variable
Parameter
Return value
feedback: An accumulator is a variable that collects a running result, such as a sum, as a loop repeats.

question: {{a}} identical candies are shared out equally among {{b}} children, giving each child as many whole candies as possible. How many candies are left over?
feedback_template: Sharing {{a}} candies among {{b}} children leaves {{expected}} over. 'What is left after equal sharing' is exactly what the remainder operator computes, written a % b in Python.

question: A Caesar cipher shifts a letter forward by {{shift}}. Letters are numbered A=0, B=1, ... Z=25, and the alphabet wraps around using modulo 26. A letter numbered {{n}} becomes which number after shifting?
feedback_template: Add the shift and wrap with modulo 26: ({{n}} + {{shift}}) % 26 = {{expected}}.

question: A lock has {{dials}} dials, and each dial has {{positions}} possible settings. In the worst case, how many combinations must a brute-force search try?
feedback_template: Each dial multiplies the possibilities, so the search space is {{positions}} to the power of {{dials}} = {{expected}}. This is why brute force gets slow fast — Enigma had about 158 million million million settings.

question: You are playing a guessing game. The secret number is somewhere from 1 to {{n}}, and after each guess you are told only "higher" or "lower". If you always guess the middle of the range that is still possible, how many guesses do you need in the worst case?
feedback_template: Each guess throws away half of what is left, so the count is how many times {{n}} candidates can be halved before just one remains: {{expected}} guesses. Guessing one number at a time instead would take up to {{n}}.

question: A brute-force program looks for duplicates in a list of {{n}} names by comparing every possible pair of names once. How many pairs does it compare?
feedback_template: Each of the {{n}} names can be paired with the other {{n}} minus 1 names, but that counts every pair from both ends, so halve it: {{expected}} comparisons. Notice how fast this grows as the list gets longer.

question: A program cracks a phone by trying every 4-digit PIN from 0000 to 9999. If the phone switches to 8-digit PINs, how does the worst-case number of tries change?
correct: It grows by a factor of 10,000, since each added digit multiplies the count by ten
incorrect: It doubles, because the PIN being cracked is now twice as long as before
It grows by 10,000 more tries, one for each combination of the new digits
It stays the same, because a brute-force search stops at the first match
feedback: Brute-force cost multiplies rather than adds: 10,000 possibilities become 100,000,000. Stopping at the first match shortens the average run but not the worst case, which is what security depends on.

question: What does the Caesar cipher do to a message?
correct: Shifts each letter a fixed number of positions through the alphabet
incorrect: Replaces each letter with a completely random and unrelated symbol
Removes the vowels from the message and keeps the remaining letters
Reverses the order of the letters, from the end back to the start
feedback: A Caesar cipher encrypts by shifting every letter by the same fixed amount, wrapping around at the end of the alphabet.

question: What was Charles Babbage's Analytical Engine (designed in the 1840s)?
correct: A mechanical, general-purpose computing machine driven by gears and punch cards
incorrect: A mechanical adding machine limited to addition and subtraction
A punch-card tabulator built to speed up counting a national census
A working electronic machine that ran stored programs in the 1940s
feedback: The Analytical Engine was a mechanical, programmable computer designed in the 1840s. It used gears and punch cards and was never fully built in Babbage's lifetime.

question: Early computers used punch cards primarily to:
correct: Feed instructions and data in as patterns of punched holes
incorrect: Record a program as magnetized spots the reader could erase later
Wire the machine's circuits into a new configuration for each job
Translate a program written in English into the machine's own code
feedback: Punch cards encoded data and instructions as patterns of holes, an idea borrowed from automated weaving looms.

question: Which of these switching technologies did computers use earliest?
correct: Vacuum tube
incorrect: Transistor
Integrated circuit
Electromechanical relay
feedback: Vacuum tubes (1940s) came first, then transistors (1947), then integrated circuits (late 1950s-1960s), each packing more switches into less space.

question: Why was the transistor (1947) such an important improvement over the vacuum tube?
correct: It was smaller, faster, and used far less power
incorrect: It was the first device able to switch a signal
It cut the cost of a machine without shrinking its size
It made vacuum tubes run cooler inside the same machine
feedback: Transistors replaced bulky, hot, failure-prone vacuum tubes with small, efficient switches, making computers smaller and more dependable.

question: What is an integrated circuit (IC)?
correct: Many transistors and other parts built onto a single chip
incorrect: A single transistor sealed in its own plastic package
A circuit board with separate chips wired together
The wiring that carries power between a chip and its board
feedback: An integrated circuit packs many transistors onto one small chip, which made computers dramatically smaller, cheaper, and more powerful starting in the 1960s.

question: Arrange these computing technologies in the order they appeared, earliest to latest.
feedback: Each generation switched faster and smaller: Babbage's mechanical gears, then hot glass vacuum tubes, then the 1947 transistor, then whole circuits printed onto a single chip.

question: The small electronic switch invented in 1947 that replaced the bulky vacuum tube is called the ___.
correct: transistor
feedback: The transistor is the tiny switch at the heart of all modern electronics; packing millions onto a chip gives us today's computers.

question: Hollerith's 1890 tabulating machines read each person's census record as a pattern of punched {{1}}, while a modern chip records and switches that same information using millions of microscopic {{2}}.
feedback: The physical medium changed completely, but the job did not: both machines store information as a pattern of two-state marks, punched or not punched, on or off. Only the size and speed of the switch improved.

question: What did time-sharing make possible on early computers?
correct: Several users to interact with one computer seemingly at the same time
incorrect: One user to submit a batch of jobs and collect printouts later
Several computers to be joined so one program runs across them
One program to keep the machine to itself until it finished
feedback: Time-sharing rapidly switches a computer's attention among users, so many people can share one expensive machine as if each had it to themselves.

question: Match each computing technology to the era and trait that defined it.

pairs.definition: 1940s electronic switch that was large and hot
1947 switch that was small and power-efficient

feedback: Computing hardware shrank steadily from room-sized gears and tubes to tiny chips, and each step made new uses possible.

question: Between the 1940s and the 1970s computers went from filling a room to fitting on a desk. Which of the following help explain that change? (Select all that apply)
correct: Transistors switch using far less power and heat than vacuum tubes
An integrated circuit packs many transistors onto one small chip
incorrect: Transistors removed the need to load programs from punch cards
Integrated circuits are what allowed many users to share one machine
Vacuum tubes were gradually made smaller until they became transistors
feedback: The machines shrank because the switching element itself changed and was then integrated: tubes were bulky, hot, and power-hungry, while a chip holds thousands of cool, tiny switches. Sharing one machine among users is time-sharing, an operating-system idea rather than a hardware one, and the transistor was a new invention, not a smaller tube.

question: What is a Large Language Model (LLM)?
correct: An AI system trained on huge amounts of text to predict and generate language
incorrect: A search engine that finds and copies the best matching web page
A stored database of answers it looks up for each question asked
A program given grammar rules by hand so its sentences parse
feedback: An LLM is an AI trained on enormous text collections. It generates responses by predicting likely next words, which is why it can produce fluent but sometimes wrong answers.

question: The ELIZA effect refers to people's tendency to:
correct: Assume a program understands more than it really does because its responses sound human
incorrect: Judge a chatbot as unintelligent as soon as one of its answers is wrong
Believe a program is thinking only after it beats a person at a hard game
Grow attached to a machine because of how it looks rather than what it says
feedback: Named after a 1960s chatbot, the ELIZA effect is our tendency to read genuine understanding into a program just because its language feels human.

question: You ask an AI assistant to write code for you. According to good practice, what should you do before trusting it?
correct: Verify the code yourself by testing it and checking the logic
incorrect: Assume that it is correct simply because the AI sounds confident
Run it on your most important data right away in order to save time
Delete it immediately if it turns out to be longer than you expected
feedback: AI assistants can produce confident but incorrect code. Verification, by reading and testing the result, is the step that makes AI-assisted work trustworthy.

question: An AI assistant hands you working code for a homework problem you do not yet understand. What does responsible practice say to do next?
correct: Trace it by hand until you could explain and rewrite every line yourself
incorrect: Submit it unchanged, since running it already produced the right output
Assume it is right because the model learned from real, working projects
Ask the model how confident it is, and accept the code if it says high
feedback: A language model generates text that is likely, not text that has been checked, and its stated confidence is produced by the same guessing process as the code. One correct run also says nothing about the inputs you have not tried.

question: Which of the following are good reasons to verify code an AI assistant produces? (Select all that apply)
correct: The AI may produce confident answers that are actually wrong
You remain responsible for code you use, even if AI wrote it
Testing reveals whether the code handles your real inputs correctly
incorrect: Verifying changes the AI's training so it never errs again
Code from an AI cannot run until a human approves it
feedback: AI output can be plausible but flawed, and the person who uses it is accountable, so testing against real inputs is essential. Verifying does not retrain the model, and AI code can run whether or not it was checked.
